messages.subject: Truncated generalized poisson
parts:
Hello dear list,

I've been trying, with big help from you, to fit a generalized Poisson model for underdispersed count data, which I finally managed to do. The main ideas, which are well pointed out by Scollnik in this paper http://www.actuaries.org/LIBRARY/ASTIN/vol28no1/135.pdf , are namely: when the are negatives values of lambda the pmf of the distribution is no longer normalized (does not sum to one), so this distribution should be normalized to solve this issue. The normalization is based on the sumation of probabilities of observing counts ranging from 0 to m, where m is the upper bound in the number of "observable" counts. m could be fixed to be given known number, M, or could also be distribution, such as m~uniform(1, M), or even m ~ poisson(mu).
Now my questions are
1) How to normalize the probabilities?
2) How to use a distribution of the parameter m in this model. I understand that in Stan it's not possible to use distribution of integers in a model

Finally, in a perhaps different subject, how to obtain WAIC once a model is fit, to do model comparison. I tried to get the likelihoods with the package RMK discrete, but it generated lots of NAs, I suppose this is related with the fact that my distribution is not normalized(?) Anyway, perhaps there's a better way to do this.

I'd appreciate any help with this subject.

Thanks,

Tada

Below is the code and data I've used to run a model in which the distribution is not truncated:

functions{
real lb(matrix X, vector beta){
real max_mu = max(exp(X * beta));
if (max_mu <= 2) return max_mu / (max_mu - 4);
return -1;    
  }
}


data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> K;
matrix[N, K] X;
vector<lower=0>[N] y;
}
transformed data {
vector[N] ym1 = y - 1;
}

parameters {
vector[K] beta;
real<lower=lb(X, beta), upper = 1> lambda;
}


model {

vector[N] eta = X * beta;
vector[N] theta = exp(eta) * (1 - lambda);
vector[N] theta_lambda_y = theta + lambda * y;
vector[N] logyfact =  lgamma(y + 1);


target += (eta + log1m(lambda) + ym1 .* log(theta_lambda_y) - theta_lambda_y - logyfact);

lambda ~ normal(0,0.1);
beta[1] ~ normal(0,10);
beta[2:4] ~ normal(0,1);

}

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: Truncated generalized poisson
parts:
Tada,

1. 
dgenpois(0:100,-0.3, .1) / sum(dgenpois(0:100,-0.3, .1),na.rm =T)
taking sum and dividing does the normalization.

2. You should pick m beforehand. m is usually small, so you can
adjust prior and see what best suits.

My 2 cents: Just pick m, that your genpoisson behaves smoothly.

There is a package 'loo' does the WAIC for you, just write
 log_lik[i] = (eta + log1m(lambda) + ym1 .* log(theta_lambda_y) - theta_lambda_y - logyfact);

in generated quantities and later on you do waic with extract_log_lik function.

Andre

messages.subject: Re: Truncated generalized poisson
parts:
Tada,

I think Stan doesn't need a normalization, it just needs to be proportional, except a normalization constant.
If you want to do normalization, it should be done inside Stan. Sorry for confusion.
You can code a sum within Stan. If theta + m * lambda < 0 you can stop the summation.
http://finzi.psych.upenn.edu/library/VGAM/html/genpoisson.html
Now max(-1,-θ/m) ≤ lambda ≤ 1 where m (≥ 4) is the greatest positive integer satisfying θ + mλ > 0 when λ < 0 

Why you not set m = max(Y_i), the maximum over all Y, the "max" count occurring in your data?
Then run one Stan and take a look at your dispersion parameter. Is it close to the "theoretical" minimum?

You can also try the gammacount, 
http://www.leg.ufpr.br/~walmes/papercompanions/gammacount2014/papercomp.html

  real gammacount(int y , real la, real a) {
    if(y>0)
      return gamma_p(y*a, a*la) - gamma_p((y+1)*a, a*la);
    return gamma_q((y+1)*a, a*la);
  }

la = exp(mu)
a >= 0 dispersion

a ~ cauchy(0, 2);
target += log(gammacount(y, la, a));

Andre

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: Truncated generalized poisson
parts:
Tada,

the gamma function is a very expensive function. Considering the Poisson distribution for one moment:
In Stan lgamma(y+1) is omitted, since its only rely on y, which is a constant. 

And now to the generalized Poisson distribution. You can omit this also, as long as you don't change
the behavior. With varying m you would change the number of classes. And thus the function is not
"comparable" anymore, except you go for normalization, that means, the sum of prob. is 1. 

About your code:
If you rely on normalization: You have to do the summation on probability scale. You are summing on log scale.
p[i] / sum(p), where 0 <= p[i]  <= 1.
I recommend to write a function outside of Stan, eg. R and then write
a Stan function which does the same and then export this function and then compare the outputs.
You also have to test then the sum of the prob., for 0, ... n, n large enough your function goes to 1.

This is my function I used btw.
Notice that theta is on the log-scale, so

 target += generalized_poisson_log(y, la, mu);

My mu is your eta, if I'm not mistaken.
(Ignore the _log, warning its a function I wrote before the syntax change in Stan)


  real generalized_poisson_log(int y, real lambda, real log_theta) {
    real theta;
    theta <- exp(log_theta);
    return log_theta
      + (y - 1) * log(theta + y * lambda)
      - lgamma(y + 1)
      - y * lambda
      - theta;
   }

About the divergence its hard to say anything without data,
try some fake data. But I would use limit lb more... set m fixed
first to max(Y) as I recommend before and then adjust your 
lb function and have a look where your lambda goes.

Andre

If the normalization involves only a constant (i.e., doesn't
depend on parameters), then you don't need to include it
in the Stan target log density.

You may need it for other purposes like WAIC, though.

real generalized_poisson_log(int y, real lambda, real theta) { 
    real log_theta;
    log_theta = log(theta);

return log_theta
      + (y - 1) * log(theta + y * lambda) 
      - lgamma(y + 1) 
      - y * lambda 
      - theta; 
   }

target += generalized_poisson_log(y, lambda, exp(mu)*(1-lambda));

My code wasn't wrong, but sampling in Stan gets easier, when exp(mu) is the real expected value.

Andre

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Truncated generalized poisson
parts: If you're just doing
> target += generalized_poisson_log(y, lambda, exp(mu)*(1-lambda));

then you won't need the lgamma(y + 1) term, which
is expensive to compute.

And the program will be more efficient if you assign
reused terms like y * lambda to locals, as in:
> real generalized_poisson_log(int y, real lambda, real theta) {

> real y_lambda = y * lambda;
> return log(theta)
> + (y - 1) * log(theta + y_lambda)
> - lgamma(y + 1) // probably don't need this term
> - y_lambda
> - theta;
> }


Here's the original for comparison:

> On Jan 31, 2017, at 11:32 AM, andre.pfeuffer via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> real generalized_poisson_log(int y, real lambda, real theta) {
> real log_theta;
> log_theta = log(theta);
> return log_theta
> + (y - 1) * log(theta + y * lambda)
> - lgamma(y + 1)
> - y * lambda
> - theta;
> }
